In [[mathematical logic]], the '''rules of passage''' govern how [[Quantifier (logic)|quantifier]]s distribute over the basic [[logical connective]]s of [[first-order logic]].  The rules of passage govern the "passage" (translation) from any [[formula (mathematical logic)|formula]] of first-order logic to the [[logical equivalence|equivalent]] formula in [[prenex normal form]], and vice versa.

==The rules==
See Quine (1982: 119, chpt. 23). Let ''Q'' and ''Q''' denote ∀ and ∃ or vice versa. β denotes a closed formula in which ''x'' does not appear. The rules of passage then include the following sentences, whose main connective is the [[biconditional]]:

*<math> Qx[\lnot\alpha (x)] \leftrightarrow \lnot Q'x[\alpha (x)].</math>

{{col-begin}}
{{col-break}}
*<math>\ Qx[\beta \lor \alpha (x)] \leftrightarrow (\beta \lor Qx \alpha (x)).</math>
*<math>\exist x[\alpha (x) \lor \gamma (x)] \leftrightarrow (\exist x \alpha (x) \lor \exist x \gamma (x)).</math>
{{col-break}}
*<math>\ Qx[\beta \land \alpha (x)] \leftrightarrow (\beta \land Qx \alpha (x)).</math>
*<math> \forall x \, [\alpha(x) \land \gamma(x)] \leftrightarrow (\forall x \, \alpha(x) \land \forall x \, \gamma(x) ).</math>
{{col-end}}

The following conditional sentences can also be taken as rules of passage:
*<math>\exist x[\alpha (x) \land \gamma (x)] \rightarrow (\exist x \alpha (x) \land \exist x \gamma (x)).</math>
*<math>(\forall x \, \alpha(x) \lor \forall x \, \gamma(x)) \rightarrow \forall x \, [\alpha(x) \lor \gamma(x)].</math>
*<math>(\exists x \, \alpha(x) \land \forall x \, \gamma(x)) \rightarrow \exists x \, [\alpha(x) \land \gamma(x)].</math>

"Rules of passage" first appeared in French, in the writings of [[Jacques Herbrand]]. [[Willard Quine|Quine]] employed the English translation of the phrase in each edition of his ''Methods of Logic'', starting in 1950.
